title: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra Hits 97% on Real Robot Arms, Topping Gemini 4 Neon
summary: OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra hits 97% success on real robot arms, topping Gemini 4 Neon
detailed: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra scored 97% on Robocurve's RoboDojo-RC Tier 1 robot-arm benchmark when run through Codex, compared to 66% using the Inspect Robots harness.
The evaluation was averaged over 120 physical trials per harness with human graders scoring each attempt against a task rubric.
The performance gap was attributed to turn structure and tool design, as Codex built its own specialized go and grip commands rather than relying on a single static move_to tool.
OpenAI also reported that its internal Codex performance factory handled over 1,700 incident investigations over roughly three months to keep ChatGPT running faster.
sentences: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra scored 97% on Robocurve's RoboDojo-RC Tier 1 robot-arm benchmark when run through Codex, the same model's result through a rival harness called Inspect Robots was 66%, a 31-point gap that Robocurve says comes down to the tools the model builds for itself.
The evaluation firm disclosed the result on X on Tuesday and said it is retiring RoboDojo from future testing.
Both figures were averaged over 120 physical trials per harness, with a human grader scoring each attempt from 0 to 1 against a task rubric that awards partial credit for visible progress.
Tier 1 covers the six easiest of RoboDojo's 18 real-world challenges, and 97% is the highest score Robocurve has recorded for any system it has tested.
The pen-capping task, the hardest in the tier because both arms must line up precisely, separated the field.
Astra on Codex succeeded in 60% of 20 trials, double the rate of the runner-up, Gemini 4 Neon running on Antigravity.
None of the robot models tested managed to cap the pen even once.
Note: The IR+ variant, which ports Codex's tools into Inspect Robots, scored 1.00 on Stand Up Bottles at $12.72 per trial.
Robocurve researcher Drew Nguyen, writing in a Nov.
22 blog post, said the team tested two explanations for the divide.
One was that Codex prevails because the model writes its own tools; the other was that something else is at work.
Inspect Robots offers only a single control tool, move_to, which ends every turn with one call and drives the arm in a straight line at a speed fixed at the start of a run.

Codex instead built go and grip commands: go rejects unreachable targets, streams instructions at 40 Hz instead of 10 Hz, abandons the straight-line constraint and decelerates at the start and end of a movement to prevent jitter.

Codex could also issue several go commands within a single turn, which Nguyen called "extremely consequential."
In simulation, move_to reproduced nearly all of Codex's motions, with 95 of 103 runs free of meaningful errors and 6,429 of 6,543 calls, or 98%, landing exactly on target.
That pointed to turn structure rather than tool design as the decisive factor.
The team then ported Codex's tools into Inspect Robots and added a way to send multiple actions per turn, naming the result IR+.
On Stand Up Bottles, both Codex and IR+ posted a perfect 1.00.
Plain Inspect Robots reached 0.48 under the original 40-call limit and 0.745 with 200 calls.

At the Ultrafast rate, which costs three times Astra's baseline price, Codex came in at $7.05 per trial on that task, IR+ at $12.72 and plain Inspect Robots at $164.34; a context cache keeps the Codex figure affordable.
Robocurve suspects that batching several moves into one turn does most of the work, though Nguyen wrote that which part of the tool set matters most remains an open question.
The benchmark's economics cut another way.

Dream-1, the top-performing robot model in the tests, costs $0.15 per trial against $9.46 for Astra on Codex, a 63-fold difference, and completes the task in 1.4 minutes on average versus 6 minutes for Astra.
The earlier GPT-6 Astra placed a block in a bowl 19 times out of 20 but pressed a puzzle piece into a tight slot only twice in 20 attempts, according to Cryptopolitan.
The results land as OpenAI pushes Codex deeper into its own operations.

19 that Codex now helps keep ChatGPT itself running faster, through an internal system it calls a performance factory: when the service slows or throws errors, Codex takes the alert, traces the cause, drafts a fix for engineer approval and then monitors the data after release to confirm recovery.
Over roughly three months the system handled more than 1,700 incident investigations, an average of about 17 a day, and identified the true root cause in more than 600 of them.

Martin Spier, who leads ChatGPT's performance team, said the strain comes from two directions at once: more than 900 million weekly ChatGPT users as of February 2026, and engineers merging 70% more code changes per week using Codex as of October 2025.
Each release draws on the same speed budget, and the cumulative effect shows up as lag.
Spier said the old assumption that someone fully understands every change going live no longer holds at OpenAI.
Accuracy remains the constraint.
In a manual audit of 100 root-cause findings produced by the agents, only 70 held up, with the rest either needing more analysis or lacking evidence that they had found the real problem.
OpenAI's answer is an adversarial check: a separate Codex instance is assigned to overturn the first one's diagnosis.

In one documented case, an investigating agent blamed an image-download failure and declared the cause found, but the reviewer noted that the internal service responsible for locating files had recovered well before the image requests stopped failing, and sent the diagnosis back for another pass.
Proposed fixes face the same scrutiny, and every change still requires an engineer's sign-off before it ships.

For the robotics market, the RoboDojo results suggest that the harness wrapped around a model can matter as much as the model itself, and that cost per successful task, not raw capability, may decide which systems reach production.

Robocurve's decision to retire the benchmark after recording a near-ceiling score also leaves the field without its most demanding public yardstick at a moment when agentic tooling is spreading into enterprise deployments, including OpenAI's Dots agents for business customers, which run on GPT-6 Astra.
